entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Windsor Castle, located in Berkshire, England, is a royal residence whose origins trace back to around 1070 AD, under the reign of William the Conqueror. It is one of the oldest and largest inhabited castles in the world, symbolizing the power and continuity of the British monarchy. Over the centuries, Windsor Castle has served not only as a royal residence but also as a stronghold and a venue for significant events, including royal weddings and state banquets. Its strategic location near London has made it a focal point of political and cultural activities in England, influencing the royal lineage and national identity.

The castle's construction was initiated as part of the Norman Conquest, aimed at consolidating power in England. Originally built in wood and later reconstructed in stone, the castle underwent numerous expansions and renovations, particularly under Henry II in the 12th century and Queen Victoria in the 19th century. It has hosted numerous significant historical events, such as the Treaty of Windsor in 1386, which established an alliance between England and Portugal, and the public celebration of royal events, including the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953, which reinforced its status as a symbol of the monarchy.

Windsor Castle continues to shape British history as it adapts to the modern era while preserving its medieval roots. It stands as a testament to the evolution of the monarchy, reflecting the changing dynamics of British society and governance. The castle has been inherited by successive monarchs, each leaving their mark on its architecture and function. Its presence has inspired countless works of art and literature, further embedding it into the cultural fabric of the nation.
